scenes.text: Aarav, 16, stands near the driver's cabin of a Delhi Metro train. He starts a stopwatch as the train leaves Rajiv Chowk.
The train speeds up smoothly for 25 s, cruises, then brakes into the next station. He wonders: how far did we go while speeding up?
His teacher Ms Kapoor says: 'Draw the velocity–time graph. The area under it is the displacement. Everything else follows.'

steps.title: Words that must be precise
steps.body:
- **Distance**: total path length (scalar, never negative).
- **Displacement**: straight-line change in position with direction (vector). Walk 3 m east then 3 m west: distance 6 m, displacement 0.
- **Velocity** v = dx/dt (vector); **speed** = |v|.
- **Acceleration** a = dv/dt. Negative acceleration only means 'opposite to the positive direction you chose', not always 'slowing down'.

Always choose a positive direction first and stick to it for every quantity.

steps.title: Derivation for constant acceleration
steps.body:
If a is constant, a = (v − u)/t, so **v = u + at** … (1)

Displacement = area under the v–t graph = rectangle (u·t) + triangle (½·(v − u)·t) = ut + ½(at)t, so **s = ut + ½at²** … (2)

Eliminate t using t = (v − u)/a in s = (u + v)t/2: s = (v² − u²)/2a, so **v² = u² + 2as** … (3)

Distance in the nth second: sₙ = u + a(2n − 1)/2 (difference of s at t = n and t = n − 1).

These hold ONLY when acceleration is constant. If a changes with time, integrate: v = u + ∫a dt, x = x₀ + ∫v dt.

steps.title: Worked example: braking distance
steps.body:
A car moves at 72 km/h and brakes with a deceleration of 5 m/s². Find stopping time and distance.

- Convert: 72 km/h = 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s. Take motion direction positive, so a = −5 m/s², final v = 0.
- Time: 0 = 20 − 5t ⇒ t = 4 s.
- Distance: 0 = 20² − 2·5·s ⇒ s = 400/10 = 40 m.

Note: stopping distance ∝ u². Double the speed (144 km/h) and the braking distance becomes 4 × 40 = 160 m. This is why speed limits matter.

steps.title: Worked example: free fall
steps.body:
A stone is dropped from a 45 m tall building (take g = 10 m/s², downward positive, u = 0).

- Time: 45 = ½·10·t² ⇒ t² = 9 ⇒ t = 3 s.
- Speed on impact: v = 0 + 10·3 = 30 m/s.
- Distance in the 3rd second: s₃ = 0 + 10(2·3 − 1)/2 = 25 m (check: 45 − 20 = 25 ✔).

Thrown **up** at u: max height H = u²/2g, time to top u/g, total flight time 2u/g (same level), and it returns with the same speed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing km/h with m/s (multiply km/h by 5/18).
- Taking g as +10 when you chose upward as positive (it must be −10).
- Using v = u + at when acceleration is not constant.
- Reporting distance when the question asks displacement (or vice versa) after the body reverses direction.
- On a v–t graph, area **below** the time axis is negative displacement but positive distance.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A ball is thrown vertically up at 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). Find (a) maximum height, (b) time to return, (c) displacement after 3 s.

Answers: (a) 20²/(2·10) = 20 m; (b) 2·20/10 = 4 s; (c) s = 20·3 − 5·9 = 15 m above the launch point (it is on its way down).

lessons.title: Projectile motion: two motions at once

scenes.text: At a club match in Kolkata, Priya fields the ball at the boundary and throws it towards the keeper, 35 m away.
Her coach shouts, 'Throw flatter!' Her friend Lucas, visiting from Berlin where he does shot put, says, 'No—45° gives maximum range!'
Who is right? Both, partly. Physics tells us exactly when, and why a real throw differs from the ideal.

steps.title: The big idea: independence
steps.body:
Ignoring air resistance, gravity acts only vertically. So:
- **Horizontal**: constant velocity uₓ = u cos θ (aₓ = 0).
- **Vertical**: uniformly accelerated, u_y = u sin θ, a_y = −g.

Treat them as two separate 1-D problems joined by the same time t.

steps.title: Derivations (launch and landing at same height)
steps.body:
x = (u cos θ)t, y = (u sin θ)t − ½gt²

- **Time of flight**: y = 0 ⇒ T = 2u sin θ / g
- **Maximum height**: v_y = 0 ⇒ H = u² sin²θ / 2g
- **Range**: R = uₓ·T = u² sin 2θ / g, maximum u²/g at θ = 45°
- **Trajectory**: eliminate t ⇒ y = x tan θ − g x² / (2u² cos²θ), a parabola.

Angles θ and (90° − θ) give the same range (sin 2θ is the same), but different heights and times.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
u = 20 m/s at θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s².
- T = 2·20·0.5/10 = 2 s
- H = 400·0.25/20 = 5 m
- R = 400·sin 60°/10 = 40 × 0.866 ≈ 34.6 m
- Speed at the top = u cos θ = 20 × 0.866 ≈ 17.3 m/s (not zero!).

So Priya's 35 m throw at 20 m/s needs about 30° (or 60°). The flatter 30° throw arrives in 2 s; the 60° throw takes about 3.5 s. That is why her coach wants it flat.

steps.title: Horizontal launch from a height
steps.body:
A ball rolls off an 80 m cliff at 15 m/s horizontally (g = 10).
- Vertical: 80 = ½·10·t² ⇒ t = 4 s (same as if dropped!).
- Horizontal distance: 15 × 4 = 60 m.
- Impact velocity: vₓ = 15, v_y = 40 ⇒ v = √(225 + 1600) ≈ 42.7 m/s at tan⁻¹(40/15) ≈ 69° below horizontal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using R = u² sin 2θ/g when launch and landing heights differ (e.g., a shot put released at 2 m height—optimal angle is then a little below 45°).
- Saying velocity is zero at the top. Only the vertical component is.
- Forgetting that real air drag reduces range and makes the path asymmetric.
- Mixing degree and radian mode on your calculator.

Answer: same range (sin 30° = sin 150°); the 75° ball stays longer because T ∝ sin θ.

scenes.text: In a Pune supermarket, Sneha pushes a loaded trolley. It refuses to move at first, then suddenly rolls.
Later, in the lift, she stands on a weighing scale (an experiment for her school project). It reads 72 kg as the lift starts up—but she weighs 60 kg!
Her elder brother draws boxes and arrows: 'Every problem is just a free-body diagram and ΣF = ma.'

steps.title: The three laws, properly
steps.body:
- **First law (inertia)**: a body stays at rest or uniform velocity unless a net external force acts. It defines **inertial frames** (non-accelerating).
- **Second law**: F_net = dp/dt; for constant mass, **F_net = ma**. Vector law—apply along each axis.
- **Third law**: forces come in pairs, equal and opposite, **acting on different bodies** and of the same type (e.g., both gravitational, both contact).

Impulse = F·Δt = Δp. That is why airbags and bending your knees when landing reduce force: they increase Δt.

steps.title: The free-body diagram (FBD) method
steps.body:
1. Isolate one body. Draw it as a dot or box.
2. Draw every force ON it: weight mg (down), normal N (perpendicular to surface), tension T (along string, away from body), friction f (along surface), applied forces.
3. Choose axes (along and perpendicular to motion/incline).
4. Write ΣF = ma along each axis.
5. Add constraint equations (same string ⇒ same acceleration magnitude).
6. Solve; check units and limiting cases.

steps.title: Atwood machine
steps.body:
Masses m₁ = 3 kg and m₂ = 2 kg hang over a light frictionless pulley (g = 10).
- m₁: m₁g − T = m₁a; m₂: T − m₂g = m₂a.
- Add: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) = 10/5 = 2 m/s².
- T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 2·3·2·10/5 = 24 N.

Check: if m₁ = m₂, a = 0 and T = mg ✔.

steps.title: Sneha's lift and the smooth incline
steps.body:
**Lift**: the scale reads the normal force N. Lift accelerating up at a: N − mg = ma ⇒ N = m(g + a). For 60 kg, a = 2 m/s²: N = 720 N, so the scale (calibrated in kg with g = 10) shows 72 kg. Accelerating down: N = m(g − a). Free fall: N = 0 (weightlessness).

**Smooth incline** of angle θ: along the plane mg sin θ = ma ⇒ a = g sin θ; perpendicular N = mg cos θ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Action and reaction cancel.' They never cancel because they act on different bodies.
- Writing 'ma' as an extra force on the FBD (in an inertial frame it is the result, not a force).
- Assuming N = mg always. On inclines, in lifts, or with vertical pushes it is different.
- Forgetting that a massless string has the same tension throughout (only if the pulley is light and frictionless).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A 5 kg block is pulled on a smooth floor by a 20 N force at 37° above horizontal (cos 37° = 0.8, sin 37° = 0.6, g = 10). Find a and N.

Answers: a = 20·0.8/5 = 3.2 m/s²; N = 50 − 20·0.6 = 38 N.

scenes.text: Rohan rides his scooter onto a curved flyover in Mumbai after rain. He feels the bike wanting to slide outward.
Engineer Farah explains that the road is banked—tilted inward—so part of the normal force provides the centripetal force.
'Wet roads lower friction,' she adds. 'That changes your safe speed. Let's calculate it.'

steps.title: Friction laws
steps.body:
- **Static friction** adjusts itself up to a maximum: f_s ≤ μ_s N. It opposes the *tendency* of relative motion.
- **Kinetic friction**: f_k = μ_k N, usually μ_k < μ_s (that's why the trolley 'jumps' once it starts).
- Friction is (approximately) independent of contact area.
- **Angle of repose**: a block just starts sliding on an incline when tan θ = μ_s.
- On a rough incline sliding down: a = g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ).

steps.title: Circular motion basics
steps.body:
Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing direction, so there is acceleration towards the centre: **a_c = v²/r = ω²r**. Net inward force needed: **F_c = mv²/r**.

'Centripetal force' is not a new force—it is the name for whatever net force points inward: friction (car on a flat road), tension (stone on a string), gravity (satellite), normal-force components (banked road).

steps.title: Flat and banked roads
steps.body:
**Flat road**: friction provides mv²/r ≤ μmg ⇒ **v_max = √(μrg)**. r = 50 m, μ = 0.4, g = 10: v_max = √200 ≈ 14.1 m/s ≈ 51 km/h.

**Banked, frictionless**: N sin θ = mv²/r, N cos θ = mg ⇒ **tan θ = v²/(rg)**. For v = 20 m/s, r = 100 m: tan θ = 0.4 ⇒ θ ≈ 21.8°.

**Banked with friction**: v_max = √[rg(μ + tan θ)/(1 − μ tan θ)].

steps.title: Vertical circle (string or loop)
steps.body:
A stone of mass m on a string of length r in a vertical circle:
- At the top: T + mg = mv²/r. Minimum speed (T = 0): **v_top = √(gr)**.
- Using energy conservation, minimum speed at the bottom: **v_bottom = √(5gr)**.
- Tension at the bottom in that case: T = mg + mv²/r = 6mg.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding 'centrifugal force' while working in the ground (inertial) frame. Use it only if you deliberately work in the rotating frame.
- Writing friction = μN when the body is not sliding—static friction may be less than its maximum.
- Saying friction always opposes motion. When you walk, friction on your foot points **forward**.
- Using diameter instead of radius.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A coin placed 10 cm from the centre of a turntable just starts slipping at ω = 5 rad/s (g = 10). Find μ_s.

Answer: μg = ω²r ⇒ μ = 25 × 0.1/10 = 0.25.

statements.s: Static friction always equals μ_s N.
statements.why: It is self-adjusting up to μ_s N; it equals μ_s N only at the point of slipping.

statements.s: Centripetal force is a separate force that appears in circular motion.
statements.why: It is the net inward resultant of real forces like friction, tension or gravity.

statements.s: Safe speed on a flat curve does not depend on the vehicle's mass.
statements.why: v_max = √(μrg): mass cancels.

statements.s: Minimum speed at the top of a vertical circle on a string is √(gr).
statements.why: At the limit T = 0, so mg = mv²/r.

statements.s: When you walk, friction on your shoe points backward.
statements.why: Your foot pushes the ground backward; ground friction pushes you forward.

scenes.text: Kavya, in Class 11 in Jaipur, tries to open the heavy wooden door of her grandmother's haveli by pushing near the hinges. It barely moves.
She pushes at the handle instead—same effort, and the door swings easily.
Her grandmother laughs: 'The carpenter knew physics. Distance from the hinge matters.' Kavya decides to find out exactly how much.

steps.title: Torque: the turning effect
steps.body:
**Torque τ = r × F**, magnitude τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the axis to the point of application and θ the angle between r and F. Unit N·m.

Equivalent: τ = F × (perpendicular distance from axis to the line of force) — the 'lever arm'.

Push at the handle (r = 0.9 m) instead of near the hinge (r = 0.1 m): nine times the torque for the same force.

Rotational analogue of Newton's second law: **τ_net = Iα** (α = angular acceleration).

steps.title: Moment of inertia I
steps.body:
I = Σ mᵢrᵢ² (or ∫r² dm). It measures how mass is distributed about the axis, not just how much there is.

Standard results (mass M, radius R, length L):
- Ring about its axis: MR²
- Disc / solid cylinder about its axis: ½MR²
- Solid sphere about a diameter: (2/5)MR²
- Thin hollow sphere: (2/3)MR²
- Thin rod about its centre (perpendicular): ML²/12; about one end: ML²/3

Radius of gyration k: I = Mk².

steps.title: Two theorems
steps.body:
- **Parallel axis**: I = I_cm + Md² (d = distance between the parallel axes). Rod about its end: ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3 ✔.
- **Perpendicular axis** (flat laminas only): I_z = I_x + I_y. For a disc, I about a diameter = ½ × ½MR² = ¼MR².

steps.title: Worked example: pulling a string on a disc
steps.body:
A disc (M = 2 kg, R = 0.5 m) pivoted at its centre has a string wound on its rim, pulled with F = 10 N.
- I = ½ × 2 × 0.25 = 0.25 kg·m²
- τ = FR = 10 × 0.5 = 5 N·m
- α = τ/I = 20 rad/s²
- After 2 s from rest: ω = αt = 40 rad/s; angle θ = ½αt² = 40 rad.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the length of r instead of the perpendicular lever arm.
- Applying the perpendicular axis theorem to 3-D bodies (it is only for planar laminas).
- Forgetting that I depends on the axis—'the moment of inertia of a rod' has no meaning without an axis.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
Find I of a ring (M, R) about a tangent in its plane.

Answer: about a diameter = ½MR² (perpendicular-axis theorem); parallel shift by R: ½MR² + MR² = (3/2)MR².

scenes.text: Ananya practises figure skating at an indoor rink in Gurugram. When she pulls her arms in, she spins much faster.
Her friend Yuki, on a video call from Sapporo, races a ball and a ring down a slope for a science fair. The ball wins every time.
Same slope, same mass. Why do shape and arm position matter? Angular momentum and rotational energy answer both.

steps.title: Angular momentum and its conservation
steps.body:
For a rigid body about a fixed axis, **L = Iω**. In general L = r × p, and τ_ext = dL/dt.

If the net external torque is zero, **L is conserved**: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂.

Ananya: arms out I₁ = 4 kg·m², ω₁ = 2 rad/s. Arms in I₂ = 1.6 kg·m² ⇒ ω₂ = 4 × 2/1.6 = 5 rad/s.

Note her kinetic energy rises: ½·4·4 = 8 J → ½·1.6·25 = 20 J. The extra comes from the work her muscles do pulling her arms in.

steps.title: Rolling without slipping
steps.body:
Condition: **v_cm = ωR** (the contact point is momentarily at rest).

Kinetic energy = translational + rotational = ½Mv² + ½Iω² = ½Mv²(1 + k²/R²).

Rolling down an incline of height h from rest: Mgh = ½Mv²(1 + k²/R²) ⇒ v = √[2gh/(1 + k²/R²)], and acceleration **a = g sin θ/(1 + k²/R²)**.

steps.title: The race down the slope
steps.body:
k²/R² values: solid sphere 2/5, disc 1/2, hollow sphere 2/3, ring 1.
- Solid sphere: a = (5/7) g sin θ
- Disc: a = (2/3) g sin θ
- Hollow sphere: a = (3/5) g sin θ
- Ring: a = (1/2) g sin θ

The solid sphere wins because less of its energy goes into rotation. Mass and radius do not matter—only shape (k/R).

steps.title: Energy split
steps.body:
A solid cylinder (disc) rolls at v. Translational KE = ½Mv²; rotational KE = ½ × ½MR² × (v/R)² = ¼Mv². So translational : rotational = 2 : 1, total = ¾Mv².

For a ring the split is 1 : 1; for a solid sphere 5 : 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using conservation of angular momentum when an external torque acts (e.g., friction from an axle).
- Assuming kinetic energy is conserved when L is conserved—it usually isn't.
- Forgetting rotational KE in rolling problems (then everything 'arrives' at √(2gh)).
- Applying v = ωR when the body slips.

steps.body:

Answer: v = √[2gh/(1 + ½)] = √(30/1.5) = √20 ≈ 4.47 m/s.

scenes.text: In her Chennai kitchen, Lakshmi's pressure cooker whistles. Her son Karthik asks where the energy from the flame goes.
Earlier he noticed his bicycle pump getting warm when he pumped hard. 'Is that the same physics?'
Yes—both are about how heat, work and internal energy trade with each other. That bookkeeping is the first law.

steps.title: The law and sign convention
steps.body:
**Q = ΔU + W**, where Q = heat given TO the system, W = work done BY the system, ΔU = change in internal energy. (Some books write ΔU = Q + W_on; same physics, different sign of W.)

Work by a gas: W = ∫P dV (area under the P–V curve). Expansion: W > 0; compression: W < 0.

For an ideal gas, U depends only on temperature: **ΔU = nC_vΔT** for ANY process.

Molar heats: C_p − C_v = R (Mayer's relation), γ = C_p/C_v. Monatomic: C_v = 3R/2, γ = 5/3. Diatomic (room temperature): C_v = 5R/2, γ = 7/5.

steps.title: The four standard processes
steps.body:
- **Isochoric** (V const): W = 0, Q = ΔU = nC_vΔT.
- **Isobaric** (P const): W = PΔV = nRΔT, Q = nC_pΔT.
- **Isothermal** (T const): ΔU = 0, Q = W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁).
- **Adiabatic** (Q = 0): PV^γ = constant, TV^(γ−1) = constant, W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1) = −ΔU.

On a P–V diagram, an adiabatic curve is steeper than an isothermal one through the same point (slope −γP/V vs −P/V).

steps.title: Worked example: isobaric heating
steps.body:
2 mol of a monatomic ideal gas is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 400 K (R = 8.314 J/mol·K).
- ΔU = nC_vΔT = 2 × 1.5 × 8.314 × 100 ≈ 2494 J
- W = nRΔT = 2 × 8.314 × 100 ≈ 1663 J
- Q = nC_pΔT = 2 × 2.5 × 8.314 × 100 ≈ 4157 J

Check: ΔU + W = 4157 ✔. Of the heat supplied, 60% raises internal energy, 40% does work.

steps.title: Why the pump gets hot
steps.body:
Quick compression is nearly adiabatic: Q ≈ 0, W < 0 (work done ON the gas), so ΔU = −W > 0: temperature rises. Diesel engines use this—compression alone heats air enough to ignite fuel.

Conversely, gas escaping fast from a spray can cools (expansion does work, ΔU < 0).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing sign conventions within one problem.
- Saying 'isothermal means no heat flow'. Isothermal: ΔT = 0; heat flows and equals work. Adiabatic: no heat flow.
- Using ΔU = nC_pΔT. Internal energy change always uses C_v.
- Using °C where kelvin is needed (PV = nRT, ratios of temperatures).

Answer: ΔU = 0 for a cycle, so W = Q_net = 200 J (= area enclosed by the loop on the P–V diagram).

lessons.title: Second law, heat engines and refrigerators

story.title: The power plant and the fridge

scenes.text: Vikram, an engineering intern at a coal power station in Maharashtra, learns that only about a third of the fuel's energy becomes electricity.
At home his sister Isha asks why the back of their refrigerator is hot if it is supposed to make things cold.
Both answers come from the second law: heat flows naturally from hot to cold, and no engine converts heat entirely into work.

steps.title: Statements of the second law
steps.body:
- **Kelvin–Planck**: no cyclic engine can convert all absorbed heat into work; some must be rejected to a colder reservoir.
- **Clausius**: heat cannot flow by itself from a colder body to a hotter one; a refrigerator needs work input.

The two are equivalent. The law introduces **entropy**: for an isolated system it never decreases.

steps.title: Engines and refrigerators
steps.body:
A **heat engine** takes Q_h from a hot reservoir, does W, rejects Q_c: W = Q_h − Q_c, efficiency **η = W/Q_h = 1 − Q_c/Q_h**.

A **Carnot engine** (reversible: two isothermal + two adiabatic steps) is the most efficient between two temperatures: **η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h** (kelvin!).

**Refrigerator**: W in, extracts Q_c from inside, dumps Q_h = Q_c + W outside (that's the hot back coil). Coefficient of performance **COP = Q_c/W**; ideal (Carnot) COP = T_c/(T_h − T_c).

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) Carnot engine between 500 K and 300 K: η = 1 − 300/500 = 0.40 (40%). If Q_h = 1000 J per cycle, W = 400 J, Q_c = 600 J.

2) An ideal refrigerator keeps its inside at 273 K in a 303 K room: COP = 273/30 = 9.1. To remove 910 J it needs only 100 J of work and dumps 1010 J into the room.

steps.title: Why real plants are well below Carnot
steps.body: Friction, heat leaks and finite-time (irreversible) processes all waste energy. Real plants also cannot use arbitrarily high temperatures because of material limits. This is why combined-cycle plants and co-generation (using waste heat) improve overall efficiency.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in 1 − T_c/T_h (e.g., 1 − 27/227 is wrong; use 300/500).
- Thinking COP cannot exceed 1. COP is not an efficiency; values of 3–10 are normal.
- Believing an open fridge door cools a room. It heats the room overall because the motor's work also becomes heat.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
An engine claims 60% efficiency between 400 K and 200 K. Is it possible?

Answer: Carnot limit = 1 − 200/400 = 50%. The claim violates the second law.

lessons.title: Electric charge, field and Gauss's law

scenes.text: On a dry January night in Delhi, Meera pulls off her woollen sweater and hears crackles. Her hair stands up.
Her little brother rubs a balloon on his hair and sticks it to the wall. 'Magic!' he declares.
Meera, preparing for her Class 12 boards, knows it is charge transfer—and decides to calculate how strong these forces really are.

steps.title: Charge and Coulomb's law
steps.body:
- Charge is **quantised** (q = ne, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) and **conserved**.
- Rubbing transfers electrons; it does not create charge.
- **Coulomb's law**: F = k q₁q₂/r², k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². Like charges repel, unlike attract.
- **Superposition**: total force = vector sum of individual forces.

steps.title: Electric field
steps.body:
E = F/q₀ (force per unit positive test charge). Point charge: **E = kq/r²**, radially outward for +q.

**Electric dipole** (charges ±q separated by 2a, p = q·2a, pointing from − to +):
- Axial point (far): E = 2kp/r³
- Equatorial point (far): E = kp/r³, opposite to p
- In a uniform field: torque τ = pE sin θ, net force zero.

steps.title: Gauss's law and its power
steps.body:
Flux through any closed surface Φ = ∮E·dA = q_enclosed/ε₀.

Choose a symmetric 'Gaussian surface' to find E quickly:
- Infinite line charge λ: E = λ/(2πε₀r)
- Infinite plane sheet σ: E = σ/(2ε₀), independent of distance
- Uniformly charged thin spherical shell (Q, R): outside E = kQ/r²; inside **E = 0**
- Conductors: E = 0 inside; charge resides on the surface (electrostatic shielding—why a car body protects you in lightning).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Charges +2 μC and +3 μC are 30 cm apart.

F = 9×10⁹ × (2×10⁻⁶)(3×10⁻⁶)/(0.3)² = 9×10⁹ × 6×10⁻¹²/0.09 = 0.6 N (repulsive).

Where between them is the field zero? Let x be the distance from 2 μC: 2/x² = 3/(0.3 − x)² ⇒ (0.3 − x)/x = √1.5 ≈ 1.225 ⇒ x ≈ 0.135 m = 13.5 cm from the 2 μC charge (closer to the smaller charge).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to convert μC (×10⁻⁶) and cm (×10⁻²).
- Adding field magnitudes from different charges without considering direction.
- Thinking Gauss's law fails for asymmetric cases—it always holds; it is just not *useful* for finding E without symmetry.
- Net flux depends only on enclosed charge; outside charges change E on the surface but not the net flux.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
A charge q sits at the centre of a cube. What is the flux through one face?

Answer: total q/ε₀ shared equally by 6 faces ⇒ q/(6ε₀).

A 1.5 V battery somehow produces a flash needing hundreds of volts. The secret: a capacitor charged slowly, discharged in a millisecond.
Dev wants to know how much energy that tiny capacitor stores.

steps.title: Electric potential
steps.body:
Potential V = work done per unit charge to bring a test charge from infinity: point charge **V = kq/r** (a scalar—just add with signs).

- Potential energy of two charges: U = kq₁q₂/r.
- E = −dV/dr: the field points from high to low potential.
- Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines; no work is done moving along them.
- 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (energy gained by an electron across 1 V).

steps.title: Capacitors
steps.body:
C = Q/V (farad). Parallel-plate: **C = ε₀A/d**; with a dielectric of constant K filling the gap: C = Kε₀A/d.

- **Series**: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + … (same charge on each)
- **Parallel**: C = C₁ + C₂ + … (same voltage on each)
- **Energy**: U = ½CV² = Q²/(2C) = ½QV; energy density u = ½ε₀E².

steps.title: Worked example: series pair
steps.body:
2 μF and 3 μF in series across 10 V.
- C_eq = (2 × 3)/(2 + 3) = 1.2 μF
- Q = C_eq V = 12 μC (same on both)
- V₁ = 12/2 = 6 V, V₂ = 12/3 = 4 V (the smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage)
- Energy stored = ½ × 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 = 60 μJ.

steps.title: Inserting a dielectric
steps.body:
A capacitor is charged and the battery is **disconnected** (Q fixed). Inserting a dielectric K: C → KC, V → V/K, U = Q²/2C → U/K (energy decreases; the slab is pulled in).

With the battery **connected** (V fixed): C → KC, Q → KQ, U → KU.

steps.title: Common mistakes and safety
steps.body:
- Using the resistor rules for capacitors (they're reversed: capacitors add in parallel).
- Treating potential as a vector.
- Forgetting whether the battery stays connected when geometry changes.
- Large capacitors (in TVs, inverters, flashes) can hold dangerous charge even after unplugging—never touch their terminals.

scenes.text: In Lucknow's peak winter, Arjun plugs a room heater and an iron into the same cheap extension board.
The board's plug gets hot and smells of melting plastic. His mother switches everything off at once.
Arjun wants to understand: what current was flowing, and why did the wire heat up?

steps.title: Current, drift and resistance
steps.body:
- Current I = dQ/dt = nAev_d (n = free electrons per m³, v_d = drift speed, typically only a fraction of a mm/s; the *signal* travels close to light speed).
- **Ohm's law**: V = IR (for ohmic conductors at constant temperature).
- **R = ρL/A**; resistivity ρ depends on material and temperature (for metals ρ rises with T).
- Stretching a wire to n times its length (volume constant) makes R → n²R.

steps.title: Combinations, EMF and power
steps.body:
- Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + … (same current). Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … (same voltage).
- A cell has EMF ε and internal resistance r: **I = ε/(R + r)**, terminal voltage **V = ε − Ir**.
- **Power** P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Energy in kWh ('units' on your bill): 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

steps.title: Kirchhoff's laws and the Wheatstone bridge
steps.body:
- **Junction law** (charge conservation): ΣI in = ΣI out.
- **Loop law** (energy conservation): ΣΔV around any closed loop = 0. Through a resistor along the current: −IR; through a cell from − to +: +ε.
- **Wheatstone bridge** P, Q, R, S: the galvanometer shows no current when **P/Q = R/S**. The metre bridge uses this idea.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) Battery ε = 12 V, r = 1 Ω, external R = 5 Ω: I = 12/6 = 2 A, terminal V = 12 − 2 = 10 V, power in R = 4 × 5 = 20 W.

2) Arjun's board at 230 V: heater 2000 W draws 2000/230 ≈ 8.7 A; iron 1000 W draws ≈ 4.3 A. Total ≈ 13 A. A board rated 6 A heats up (P = I²R in its thin wires and loose contacts) and can catch fire.

steps.title: Common mistakes and safety
steps.body:
- Assuming ε equals terminal voltage when current flows.
- Wrong signs in loop equations—pick a direction and be consistent; a negative answer just means current flows the other way.
- Never overload sockets; use correctly rated boards and MCBs; never bypass a fuse with ordinary wire.

The radiographer explains that the scanner's superconducting coils create a field tens of thousands of times stronger than Earth's.

steps.title: Force on moving charges and wires
steps.body:
- **Lorentz force**: F = q(E + v × B). Magnetic part: F = qvB sin θ, perpendicular to both v and B, so it does **no work** (speed stays constant).
- In a uniform B with v ⟂ B: circular path, **r = mv/(qB)**, period **T = 2πm/(qB)** — independent of speed (the cyclotron principle).
- **Wire**: F = I L × B, magnitude BIL sin θ. Direction: Fleming's left-hand rule or the right-hand rule for the cross product.

steps.title: Fields produced by currents
steps.body:
Biot–Savart: dB = (μ₀/4π) I dl × r̂ / r², μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A.
- Long straight wire: **B = μ₀I/(2πr)**
- Centre of a circular loop (radius R, N turns): **B = μ₀NI/(2R)**
- Long solenoid (n turns per metre): **B = μ₀nI** inside, ≈ 0 outside
- Ampère's law: ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enclosed (use for symmetric cases).
- Two parallel wires: force per length = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd); same-direction currents **attract**.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) Wire with 10 A; field 5 cm away: B = (4π×10⁻⁷ × 10)/(2π × 0.05) = 4 × 10⁻⁵ T (comparable to Earth's field, roughly 5 × 10⁻⁵ T—why a compass near a cable deflects).

2) A proton (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) at 10⁶ m/s in B = 0.1 T: r = (1.67×10⁻²⁷ × 10⁶)/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 0.1) ≈ 0.104 m.

steps.title: Current loop as a magnet; galvanometer
steps.body: A loop of area A carrying I has magnetic moment m = NIA; in field B it feels torque τ = mB sin θ. The moving-coil galvanometer uses this: deflection ∝ current. Convert it to an **ammeter** with a small shunt in parallel; to a **voltmeter** with a large resistance in series.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a magnetic field can speed up a charge. It only changes direction.
- Using the right-hand rule for electrons without reversing the direction (negative charge).
- Confusing turns per metre (n) with total turns (N) in the solenoid formula.

Answer: n = 1000 per m; B = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 1000 × 2 ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻³ T.

scenes.text: Selvi's uncle works at a wind farm near Kanyakumari. Each giant turbine spins a generator that pushes electricity into the grid.
At home, her family cooks on an induction cooktop that stays fairly cool to the touch while the steel pan gets hot.
Both are Faraday's discovery at work: a changing magnetic flux induces an EMF.

steps.title: Faraday and Lenz
steps.body:
Magnetic flux Φ = B·A = BA cos θ (weber).
- **Faraday**: ε = −N dΦ/dt.
- **Lenz**: the induced current opposes the change that produces it (the minus sign; energy conservation).
- **Motional EMF**: a rod of length l moving at v perpendicular to B: ε = Blv.
- Rotating coil (generator): ε = NBAω sin ωt, peak ε₀ = NBAω.
- Eddy currents: induced currents in bulk metal—used in induction cooking and magnetic braking; reduced in transformers by laminated cores.

steps.title: Inductance
steps.body: Self-inductance: ε = −L dI/dt; long solenoid L = μ₀n²Al. Energy stored U = ½LI². Mutual inductance couples two coils (the basis of transformers).

steps.title: Alternating current essentials
steps.body:
- V = V₀ sin ωt; **V_rms = V₀/√2**. Indian mains: 230 V rms, 50 Hz ⇒ peak ≈ 325 V.
- Reactances: X_L = ωL, X_C = 1/(ωC).
- Series LCR impedance: **Z = √[R² + (X_L − X_C)²]**, phase tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R.
- **Resonance** at ω₀ = 1/√(LC): Z = R (minimum), current maximum (radio tuning).
- Average power P = V_rms I_rms cos φ (cos φ = power factor). Pure L or C: average power zero.
- **Ideal transformer**: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p = I_p/I_s. Power is transmitted at high voltage to cut I²R losses.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) A 0.5 m rod moves at 4 m/s perpendicular to B = 0.2 T: ε = 0.2 × 0.5 × 4 = 0.4 V.

2) Series LCR: R = 30 Ω, X_L = 80 Ω, X_C = 40 Ω, V_rms = 100 V. Z = √(900 + 1600) = 50 Ω; I_rms = 2 A; cos φ = 30/50 = 0.6; P = 100 × 2 × 0.6 = 120 W (= I²R ✔).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting N in Faraday's law or cos θ in flux.
- Adding R and reactances directly (they combine as phasors).
- Thinking transformers work on steady DC—they need changing flux.
- Mixing peak and rms values in power calculations.

Answer: N_s = 2000 × 11.5/230 = 100 turns.

lessons.title: Ray optics: mirrors, lenses and your eyes

scenes.text: Suresh Dadaji, 64, in Indore, can no longer read the newspaper without holding it at arm's length.
The optometrist prescribes +2.5 D reading glasses. His granddaughter Nisha asks, 'What does +2.5 even mean?'
It is the lens power in dioptres: P = 1/f with f in metres. Nisha sets out to master the lens formula.

steps.title: Reflection, refraction, TIR
steps.body:
- Mirrors: f = R/2. **Mirror formula** 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; magnification m = −v/u.
- **Snell's law**: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Light bends towards the normal entering a denser medium.
- **Total internal reflection** going dense → rare beyond the critical angle: sin C = n₂/n₁ (= 1/n into air). Glass n = 1.5: C ≈ 41.8°. Used in optical fibres; it also gives diamonds their sparkle.
- Apparent depth = real depth / n (a pool looks shallower).

steps.title: Thin lenses (Cartesian sign convention)
steps.body:
Distances are measured from the optical centre; along the incident light = positive. Object on the left ⇒ u negative.
- **Lens formula**: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f
- **Magnification**: m = v/u (negative ⇒ real, inverted)
- **Lens maker's formula**: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
- **Power** P = 1/f (f in m), unit dioptre (D). Convex +, concave −. Lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Object 30 cm in front of a convex lens of f = 20 cm: u = −30, f = +20.

1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60 ⇒ v = +60 cm. m = v/u = −2: real, inverted, twice the size, 60 cm behind the lens.

Move the object to 10 cm (inside f): 1/v = 1/20 − 1/10 = −1/20 ⇒ v = −20 cm: virtual, erect, magnified ×2 (a magnifying glass).

steps.title: Eye defects
steps.body:
- **Myopia** (near-sightedness): the image forms in front of the retina; corrected by a **concave** lens. Far point 2 m ⇒ P = −1/2 = −0.5 D.
- **Hypermetropia** (far-sightedness): corrected by a **convex** lens.
- **Presbyopia**: age-related loss of accommodation; reading glasses (convex), like Dadaji's +2.5 D (f = 40 cm).
- **Astigmatism**: corrected by cylindrical lenses.

See an optometrist or eye doctor for any vision change; this is general education.

steps.body:

- Forgetting u is negative for real objects.

- Thinking a glass lens has the same focal length in water—it increases because (n_lens/n_medium − 1) shrinks.

Her cousin's polarised sunglasses make the glare from the sea vanish—until he tilts his head.

steps.title: Huygens and interference
steps.body:
Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets (Huygens). Two coherent sources superpose:
- **Constructive** (bright): path difference Δ = nλ
- **Destructive** (dark): Δ = (n + ½)λ

**Young's double slit**: slit separation d, screen distance D. Bright fringes at y = nλD/d. **Fringe width β = λD/d**. Intensity I = 4I₀cos²(φ/2) for equal sources.

steps.title: Worked example: YDSE
steps.body:
λ = 600 nm, D = 1 m, d = 0.5 mm. β = (600×10⁻⁹ × 1)/(0.5×10⁻³) = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m = 1.2 mm.

Immerse the setup in water (n ≈ 1.33): λ becomes λ/n, so β ≈ 0.9 mm. Increase d ⇒ the fringes crowd together.

steps.title: Diffraction and resolution
steps.body:
**Single slit** of width a: minima at a sin θ = nλ (n = ±1, ±2 …). The central maximum's angular width ≈ 2λ/a — a narrower slit gives a wider spread.

Diffraction limits how fine a detail telescopes and microscopes can resolve; larger apertures and shorter wavelengths resolve better.

Thin-film colours (bubbles, oil on wet roads) come from interference between reflections at the film's two surfaces.

steps.title: Polarisation
steps.body:
Light is a transverse wave, so it can be polarised.
- **Malus's law**: I = I₀ cos²θ after an analyser at angle θ.
- Unpolarised light through one polaroid: intensity halves.
- **Brewster's law**: reflected light is fully polarised when tan θ_B = n (glass: ≈ 56°). Polarised sunglasses block this mostly horizontally polarised glare.

steps.body:

- Mixing up the double-slit maxima condition (d sin θ = nλ) with single-slit minima (a sin θ = nλ)—same form, opposite meaning.
- Forgetting the ½ factor when unpolarised light meets the first polaroid.

lessons.title: Dual nature: photoelectric effect and matter waves

scenes.text: In a Rajasthan village, Hemant watches solar street lights switch on by themselves at dusk.
In the city, his cousin Ritika notices that mall doors open as she approaches—another light sensor.
Their science teacher says these devices rely on light arriving in packets—photons. Einstein received the Nobel Prize for explaining the photoelectric effect this way.

steps.title: What the experiments showed
steps.body:
When light falls on a metal surface, electrons may be emitted. Observations that waves could not explain:
- Below a **threshold frequency** ν₀, no emission at all—however intense the light.
- The maximum kinetic energy of electrons depends on **frequency**, not intensity.
- Intensity changes only the **number** of electrons (photocurrent).
- Emission is practically instantaneous.

steps.title: Einstein's equation
steps.body:
Light consists of photons of energy **E = hν = hc/λ** (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s). Handy: E (eV) ≈ 1240/λ(nm).

**K_max = hν − φ**, where the work function φ = hν₀. Stopping potential: eV₀ = K_max.

The graph of V₀ versus ν is a straight line with slope h/e and intercept ν₀—the same slope for every metal.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Metal with φ = 2.0 eV, light of 400 nm.
- E = 1240/400 = 3.1 eV
- K_max = 3.1 − 2.0 = 1.1 eV
- Stopping potential V₀ = 1.1 V
- Threshold wavelength λ₀ = 1240/2.0 = 620 nm (red light at 700 nm would emit nothing).

steps.title: Matter waves
steps.body: De Broglie: every particle has λ = h/p = h/(mv). For an electron accelerated through V volts: **λ ≈ 1.227/√V nm**. At 100 V, λ ≈ 0.123 nm—comparable to atomic spacings, which is why electron microscopes can resolve tiny structures. Confirmed by the Davisson–Germer experiment (electron diffraction from nickel).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying brighter light gives faster electrons (it gives more electrons).
- Forgetting to convert eV ↔ J (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).
- Using λ = h/mv for photons (use λ = h/p with p = E/c).

Answer: new photon energy 6 eV ⇒ K_max = 4 eV (it was 1 eV)—it more than doubles.

steps.title: Bohr model of hydrogen
steps.body:
Postulates: electrons move in stationary orbits with angular momentum L = nh/2π; they emit or absorb a photon only when jumping between orbits: hν = E_i − E_f.

For hydrogen-like atoms (atomic number Z):
- Radius rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z Å
- Energy **Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV**
- Wavelengths: 1/λ = R Z²(1/n_f² − 1/n_i²), R ≈ 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹.

Series: **Lyman** (to n = 1, ultraviolet), **Balmer** (to n = 2, visible), **Paschen** (to n = 3, infrared).

steps.title: Worked example: the red line
steps.body:
Hydrogen, n = 3 → n = 2: ΔE = 13.6(1/4 − 1/9) = 13.6 × 5/36 ≈ 1.89 eV. λ = 1240/1.89 ≈ 656 nm — the red Hα line of the Balmer series.

Ionisation energy from the ground state = 13.6 eV.

steps.title: Nucleus and binding energy
steps.body:
Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3) (R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm) ⇒ nuclear density is roughly the same for all nuclei.

**Mass defect** Δm = (mass of separate nucleons) − (mass of nucleus). Binding energy = Δm c²; 1 u ≈ 931.5 MeV. Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron (about 8.8 MeV), so **fission** of heavy nuclei and **fusion** of light nuclei both release energy.

steps.title: Radioactive decay
steps.body:
- α (helium nucleus): A − 4, Z − 2. β⁻ (electron + antineutrino): Z + 1. γ: no change in A or Z.
- Law: **N = N₀e^(−λt)**; half-life **T½ = ln 2/λ ≈ 0.693/λ**; mean life τ = 1/λ.
- After n half-lives, the fraction left = (½)ⁿ.

Example: 160 g of an isotope with T½ = 2 days: after 6 days (3 half-lives) 20 g remains.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Z instead of Z² in hydrogen-like energies (He⁺ ground state is −54.4 eV).
- Thinking a sample vanishes after two half-lives (¼ remains).
- Getting the mass number change wrong in β decay (A is unchanged).

Answer: α ⇒ A = 234, Z = 90; two β⁻ ⇒ Z = 92. Final: A = 234, Z = 92 (an isotope of uranium).

story.title: Riya zooms in on a speedometer

scenes.text: Riya, 16, sits beside her father on the Mumbai–Pune Expressway. The speedometer reads 80 km/h. 'But speed at one instant—how can you divide distance by zero time?' she asks.
Her father, a civil engineer, smiles: 'You don't divide by zero. You see what the average speed approaches as the time interval shrinks.'
That 'approaching' idea is a limit—the foundation of all calculus.

steps.title: What a limit means
steps.body:
lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means f(x) gets as close to L as we like when x is close enough to a (x ≠ a). The value f(a) itself does not matter—it may not even exist.

The limit exists only if the **left-hand limit = right-hand limit**.

Algebra of limits: limits of sums, products and quotients are the sums, products and quotients of the limits (provided the denominator's limit ≠ 0).

steps.title: Standard limits to know by heart
steps.body:
- lim_{x→0} (sin x)/x = 1 (x in radians)
- lim_{x→0} (1 − cos x)/x² = ½
- lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1)/x = 1; lim_{x→0} (aˣ − 1)/x = ln a
- lim_{x→0} ln(1 + x)/x = 1
- lim_{x→0} (1 + x)^{1/x} = e
- lim_{x→a} (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹

steps.title: Continuity
steps.body:
f is continuous at a if **lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a)** (the limit exists, the value exists, and they match).

Example: f(x) = kx + 1 for x ≤ 2, and 3x − 1 for x > 2. Continuity at 2: 2k + 1 = 5 ⇒ **k = 2**.

Polynomials, sin, cos and eˣ are continuous everywhere; rational functions wherever the denominator ≠ 0. A differentiable function is continuous, but |x| at 0 is continuous yet not differentiable (a corner).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using degrees in sin x/x (the limit 1 holds only in radians).
- 'Cancelling' to get a value without checking the 0/0 form.
- Concluding a limit exists from one side only.
- Writing ∞/∞ = 1 or 0/0 = 1. They are indeterminate forms.

scenes.text: Ammi pours chai at 90 °C in a Hyderabad kitchen. Faisal notices it cools fast at first, then slowly.
'How fast is it cooling right now?' he asks. The answer is a derivative—the instantaneous rate of change.
He learns a small toolkit of rules that can differentiate almost anything.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h — the slope of the tangent, the instantaneous rate.

From first principles, f(x) = x²: [(x + h)² − x²]/h = 2x + h → **2x**.

steps.title: Standard derivatives and rules
steps.body:
- d/dx xⁿ = nxⁿ⁻¹; d/dx eˣ = eˣ; d/dx ln x = 1/x; d/dx aˣ = aˣ ln a
- sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec² x; sec x → sec x tan x
- sin⁻¹x → 1/√(1 − x²); tan⁻¹x → 1/(1 + x²)
- **Product**: (uv)' = u'v + uv'; **Quotient**: (u/v)' = (u'v − uv')/v²
- **Chain**: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))·g'(x)

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1) y = x² sin x ⇒ y' = 2x sin x + x² cos x.
2) y = sin(3x² + 1) ⇒ y' = cos(3x² + 1)·6x.
3) y = e^{2x}/(1 + x) ⇒ y' = [2e^{2x}(1 + x) − e^{2x}]/(1 + x)² = e^{2x}(1 + 2x)/(1 + x)².
4) **Implicit**: x² + y² = 25 ⇒ 2x + 2yy' = 0 ⇒ y' = −x/y. At (3, 4): slope −3/4.
5) **Logarithmic**: y = xˣ ⇒ ln y = x ln x ⇒ y'/y = ln x + 1 ⇒ y' = xˣ(1 + ln x).
6) **Parametric**: x = at², y = 2at ⇒ dy/dx = (2a)/(2at) = 1/t.

steps.title: Higher derivatives
steps.body: y'' = d²y/dx². For y = e^{3x}: y' = 3e^{3x}, y'' = 9e^{3x}. In physics, if x(t) is position, x' is velocity and x'' is acceleration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the chain-rule factor (d/dx sin 2x = 2 cos 2x, not cos 2x).
- Writing (uv)' = u'v'.
- Reversing the order in the quotient-rule numerator (it is u'v − uv').
- Applying the power rule to xˣ or 2ˣ (a variable exponent needs logs).

lessons.title: Applications of derivatives: rates, maxima and minima

scenes.text: Kiran runs a small packaging business in Surat. From an 18 cm square of card, she cuts equal squares from each corner and folds up a box.
Cut too little: a flat tray. Cut too much: a tall thin box. Which cut gives the biggest volume?
Her nephew Varun, in Class 12, sets the derivative to zero and finds the answer in two lines.

steps.title: Rates of change
steps.body: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt). Example: a balloon's radius grows at 0.5 cm/s. When r = 10 cm, V = (4/3)πr³ ⇒ dV/dt = 4πr²(dr/dt) = 4π(100)(0.5) = **200π cm³/s**.

steps.title: Increasing/decreasing and extrema
steps.body:
- f' > 0 on an interval ⇒ increasing; f' < 0 ⇒ decreasing.
- Critical points: f'(c) = 0 or f' undefined.
- **First-derivative test**: f' changes + to − ⇒ local max; − to + ⇒ local min.
- **Second-derivative test**: f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) < 0 ⇒ max; > 0 ⇒ min; = 0 ⇒ the test fails.
- On a closed interval [a, b], the absolute max/min occur at critical points or endpoints—check them all.

steps.title: Kiran's box solved
steps.body:
Cut squares of side x. Box: base (18 − 2x)², height x. V = x(18 − 2x)², 0 < x < 9.

V' = (18 − 2x)² − 4x(18 − 2x) = (18 − 2x)(18 − 6x). V' = 0 ⇒ x = 3 (x = 9 gives zero volume).

Sign change: V' > 0 for x < 3 and V' < 0 for 3 < x < 9 ⇒ maximum.

**Maximum volume = 3 × 12² = 432 cm³.**

steps.title: Tangents and approximation
steps.body:
Tangent to y = x³ at (1, 1): slope 3 ⇒ y − 1 = 3(x − 1). Normal: slope −1/3.

Approximation: f(x + Δx) ≈ f(x) + f'(x)Δx. √25.1 ≈ 5 + (1/(2·5))(0.1) = 5.01.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stopping at f'(c) = 0 without checking whether it is a max or a min.
- Forgetting endpoints in closed-interval problems.
- Ignoring the domain (x must keep all dimensions positive).
- Confusing local and absolute extrema.

steps.title: Antiderivatives
steps.body:
∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C where F' = f.
- ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C (n ≠ −1); ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C
- ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C; ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C; ∫cos x dx = sin x + C; ∫sec² x dx = tan x + C
- ∫dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹ x + C; ∫dx/√(1 − x²) = sin⁻¹ x + C

steps.title: Techniques
steps.body:
- **Substitution**: ∫2x cos(x²) dx, put t = x² ⇒ ∫cos t dt = sin(x²) + C.
- **By parts**: ∫u v dx = u∫v dx − ∫(u'∫v dx)dx; choose u by ILATE (Inverse trig, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential). ∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C.
- **Partial fractions**: ∫dx/(x² − 1) = ½ ln|(x − 1)/(x + 1)| + C.
- Special: ∫eˣ[f(x) + f'(x)]dx = eˣ f(x) + C.

steps.title: Definite integrals and properties
steps.body:
**Fundamental theorem**: ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a).
- ∫₀^π sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^π = 2
- ∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x)dx. Example: I = ∫₀^{π/2} sin x/(sin x + cos x)dx; adding it to the replaced form gives 2I = π/2 ⇒ **I = π/4**.
- ∫₋ₐᵃ f = 0 if f is odd; = 2∫₀ᵃ f if f is even.

steps.title: Area between curves
steps.body:
Area between y = x and y = x² (they meet at x = 0 and 1; x ≥ x² there):

A = ∫₀¹ (x − x²)dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]₀¹ = ½ − ⅓ = **1/6 square units**.

Area of the circle x² + y² = a²: 4∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²)dx = πa² ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting + C in indefinite integrals.
- Not changing the limits after substitution in definite integrals.
- Area below the x-axis: the definite integral is negative, but area must use |f|.
- ∫(1/x)dx is ln|x|, not x⁰/0.

story.title: The bacteria and the hot car

scenes.text: Microbiology student Tara in Pune notes that a bacterial culture doubles every 3 hours.
Her friend Omar, in Dubai, wonders how quickly a hot car's interior cools after it is parked in the shade.
Both are described by equations involving rates—differential equations.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Order**: the highest derivative present. **Degree**: the power of the highest derivative when the equation is a polynomial in its derivatives.
- A general solution has as many arbitrary constants as the order; a particular solution uses given conditions.

Example: (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx) = 0 has order 2, degree 3.

steps.title: Variable separable
steps.body:
dy/dx = g(x)h(y) ⇒ ∫dy/h(y) = ∫g(x)dx.

**Growth**: dN/dt = kN ⇒ N = N₀e^{kt}. Tara's culture: doubling time 3 h ⇒ k = ln 2/3 per hour. After 9 h: N = N₀·2³ = 8N₀.

**Newton's law of cooling**: dT/dt = −k(T − Tₛ) ⇒ T = Tₛ + (T₀ − Tₛ)e^{−kt}.

steps.title: Homogeneous and linear equations
steps.body:
- **Homogeneous** dy/dx = F(y/x): substitute y = vx ⇒ v + x dv/dx = F(v), then separate.
- **Linear first order**: dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x). Integrating factor **IF = e^{∫P dx}**; solution y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C.

Example: dy/dx + y = eˣ. IF = eˣ ⇒ y eˣ = ∫e^{2x}dx = e^{2x}/2 + C ⇒ **y = eˣ/2 + Ce^{−x}**.

steps.title: Worked example: separable
steps.body:
Solve dy/dx = xy with y(0) = 2.

∫dy/y = ∫x dx ⇒ ln|y| = x²/2 + c ⇒ y = Ae^{x²/2}. y(0) = 2 ⇒ A = 2. **y = 2e^{x²/2}**.

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.body:

steps.title: Cross (vector) product
steps.body:
a × b = |a||b| sin θ n̂, where n̂ is perpendicular to both (right-hand rule).
- Determinant form: a × b = |i j k; a₁ a₂ a₃; b₁ b₂ b₃|
- a × b = −(b × a) (not commutative); a × a = 0
- i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j

steps.title: Scalar triple product
steps.body:

- |[a b c]| = volume of the parallelepiped.
- [a b c] = 0 ⇔ the vectors are **coplanar**.
- Cyclic swaps keep the value; swapping two vectors changes its sign.

Example: a = i, b = j, c = i + j + k: [a b c] = det[[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[1,1,1]] = 1 ⇒ volume 1.

scenes.text: Air-traffic trainee Meenakshi studies two flight paths in 3-D space near Delhi. They aren't parallel, but do they intersect?
If not, how close do the planes come? That shortest distance is a safety number.
Vector equations of lines make the calculation systematic.

steps.title: Equations of a line
steps.body:
Through point a with direction b: **r = a + λb**.

Cartesian: (x − x₁)/l = (y − y₁)/m = (z − z₁)/n, where (l, m, n) are direction ratios.

Through two points A and B: direction b = B − A.

Angle between two lines: cos θ = |b₁·b₂|/(|b₁||b₂|).

steps.title: Relative positions
steps.body:
- **Parallel**: b₁ ∥ b₂.
- **Intersecting**: not parallel and shortest distance 0.
- **Skew**: neither parallel nor intersecting (possible only in 3-D).

**Shortest distance between skew lines**: d = |(a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂)| / |b₁ × b₂|.

Parallel lines: d = |b × (a₂ − a₁)|/|b|.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
L₁: r = (i + j) + λ(2i − j + k); L₂: r = (2i + j − k) + μ(3i − 5j + 2k).
- b₁ × b₂ = |i j k; 2 −1 1; 3 −5 2| = 3i − j − 7k; magnitude √59
- a₂ − a₁ = i − k
- (a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂) = 3 + 0 + 7 = 10
- **d = 10/√59 ≈ 1.30 units** (non-zero, so the lines are skew).

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: Equation of a plane
steps.body:
Normal vector n and point a: **(r − a)·n = 0**, i.e., r·n = d. Cartesian: ax + by + cz = d with normal (a, b, c).

Intercept form: x/a + y/b + z/c = 1.

Through three non-collinear points: normal n = (B − A) × (C − A).

steps.title: Angles and distances
steps.body:
- Angle between planes = angle between normals: cos θ = |n₁·n₂|/(|n₁||n₂|).
- Angle between a line (direction b) and a plane (normal n): sin φ = |b·n|/(|b||n|).
- **Distance of point (x₀, y₀, z₀) from ax + by + cz = d**: |ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ − d| / √(a² + b² + c²).
- Distance between parallel planes ax + by + cz = d₁ and ax + by + cz = d₂: |d₁ − d₂|/√(a² + b² + c²).

scenes.text: Fatima runs two bakery outlets in Lucknow. Each day she records how many breads, cakes and cookies each outlet sells.
Multiplying her quantity table by a price list gives each outlet's revenue in one step.
That one-step multiplication is matrix multiplication—the language of spreadsheets, graphics and AI.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
An m × n matrix has m rows and n columns. Types: square, diagonal, identity I, zero, symmetric (Aᵀ = A), skew-symmetric (Aᵀ = −A; diagonal entries 0).

Addition: same order, entry by entry. Scalar multiple: multiply every entry.

Any square matrix = ½(A + Aᵀ) [symmetric] + ½(A − Aᵀ) [skew-symmetric].

steps.title: Multiplication
steps.body:
(AB)ᵢⱼ = row i of A · column j of B. Defined only if the columns of A = the rows of B; (m × n)(n × p) = m × p.
- **AB ≠ BA in general.**
- AB = 0 does not imply A = 0 or B = 0.
- (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ; (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying entry by entry (that is not matrix multiplication).
- Writing (AB)ᵀ = AᵀBᵀ.
- Expanding (A + B)² as A² + 2AB + B² (correct: A² + AB + BA + B²).

That gives three equations in three unknowns. 'Write it as AX = B,' says his colleague Dr Leena, 'then X = A⁻¹B if |A| ≠ 0.'
Determinants tell whether a unique mix even exists.

steps.title: Determinants
steps.body:
2 × 2: |a b; c d| = ad − bc. 3 × 3: expand along any row or column with signs + − +.

Example: |1 2 3; 0 1 4; 5 6 0| = 1(0 − 24) − 2(0 − 20) + 3(0 − 5) = −24 + 40 − 15 = **1**.

Properties: swapping two rows changes the sign; two identical rows ⇒ 0; |Aᵀ| = |A|; |AB| = |A||B|; |kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n × n matrix.

Area of the triangle with vertices (xᵢ, yᵢ) = ½|det[[x₁, y₁, 1], [x₂, y₂, 1], [x₃, y₃, 1]]|; zero ⇒ collinear.

steps.title: Inverse
steps.body:
A⁻¹ exists iff |A| ≠ 0 (non-singular). **A⁻¹ = adj(A)/|A|**, where adj A = the transpose of the cofactor matrix.

2 × 2 shortcut: [[a, b], [c, d]]⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc))[[d, −b], [−c, a]]. Example: [[2, 1], [1, 1]]⁻¹ = [[1, −1], [−1, 2]].

Useful: A·adj A = |A|I; |adj A| = |A|ⁿ⁻¹.

steps.title: Solving AX = B
steps.body:
x + y = 5, 2x − y = 1. A = [[1, 1], [2, −1]], |A| = −3 ≠ 0.

A⁻¹ = (1/−3)[[−1, −1], [−2, 1]]. X = A⁻¹B = (1/−3)[[−5 − 1], [−10 + 1]] = (1/−3)[[−6], [−9]] = [[2], [3]] ⇒ **x = 2, y = 3**.

Consistency: |A| ≠ 0 ⇒ unique solution. |A| = 0 ⇒ compute (adj A)B: if it is non-zero, there is no solution; if it is zero, the system has either infinitely many solutions or none (investigate further).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the sign pattern in cofactors.
- Forgetting to transpose the cofactor matrix to get adj A.
- Using |kA| = k|A| for a 3 × 3 matrix (it's k³|A|).
- Writing X = BA⁻¹ instead of A⁻¹B.

scenes.text: Ramesh, 45, in Mysuru gets a positive result on a screening test for a rare condition that affects 1 in 100 people. He panics.
His daughter Divya, who loves probability, asks the doctor two numbers: the test catches 99% of true cases but also flags 5% of healthy people.
Using Bayes' theorem, she finds the chance he actually has the condition is only about 1 in 6—so a confirmatory test is needed, not panic.

steps.title: Conditional probability
steps.body:
**P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B)**, P(B) > 0 — the probability of A given that B has happened.

Multiplication rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(B)·P(A|B).

**Independent** events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) (equivalently P(A|B) = P(A)). Independent ≠ mutually exclusive: mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are always dependent.

steps.title: Total probability and Bayes
steps.body:
If E₁, E₂, …, Eₙ partition the sample space:
- **Total probability**: P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ)
- **Bayes' theorem**: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) / Σ P(Eⱼ)P(A|Eⱼ)

It reverses the condition: from P(test positive | disease) to P(disease | test positive).

steps.title: Divya's calculation
steps.body:
D = has the condition, + = positive test. P(D) = 0.01, P(+|D) = 0.99, P(+|not D) = 0.05.
- P(+) = 0.01 × 0.99 + 0.99 × 0.05 = 0.0099 + 0.0495 = 0.0594
- P(D|+) = 0.0099/0.0594 = **1/6 ≈ 16.7%**

Intuition with 10 000 people: 100 have it, 99 test positive; 9 900 don't, 495 test positive. Of 594 positives, only 99 are true.

steps.title: Classic: bags and balls
steps.body:
Bag I: 3 red, 4 black. Bag II: 5 red, 6 black. A bag is chosen at random and a red ball is drawn. P(Bag I | red)?

P(red) = ½·3/7 + ½·5/11 = (33 + 35)/154 = 68/154. P(I|red) = (3/14)/(68/154) = (3/14)(154/68) = 33/68.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A) (the 'prosecutor's fallacy').
- Ignoring the base rate (prior) when interpreting tests.
- Treating mutually exclusive events as independent.
- Health note: screening results should always be interpreted by a doctor; this lesson is about mathematics, not medical advice.

scenes.text: Neha, captain of her school basketball team in Shillong, makes 70% of her free throws. In a match she takes 5.
Coach Lyngdoh asks: what's the chance she makes at least 4? And how many should we expect on average?
The binomial distribution answers both.

steps.title: Random variables
steps.body:
A random variable X assigns numbers to outcomes. A probability distribution lists values xᵢ with P(xᵢ) ≥ 0 and ΣP = 1.
- **Mean** E(X) = Σ xᵢpᵢ
- **Variance** Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]²; SD = √Var

Example: a fair die: E(X) = 3.5, E(X²) = 91/6, Var = 91/6 − 12.25 = 35/12.

steps.title: Bernoulli trials and the binomial
steps.body:
Conditions: a fixed number n of independent trials, each a success with the same probability p (q = 1 − p).

**P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ**, r = 0, 1, …, n. **Mean = np, variance = npq.**

steps.title: Coins
steps.body: 10 fair coins. P(exactly 6 heads) = ¹⁰C₆/2¹⁰ = 210/1024 ≈ 0.205. P(at least one head) = 1 − (½)¹⁰ = 1023/1024. Use the complement for 'at least one'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the binomial when trials are not independent (drawing cards without replacement).
- Forgetting the ⁿCᵣ factor.
- Adding standard deviations instead of variances.
- Computing 'at least one' directly instead of 1 − P(none).

scenes.text: Anaya, 15, in Thiruvananthapuram, scrapes the inside of her cheek with a clean toothpick and looks at it under her school microscope.
Next to it is a slide of onion peel. The onion cells look like neat bricks with thick walls; her cheek cells look like irregular flat pebbles.
'Why the difference?' she asks Mrs Thomas. 'Because plants and animals solved the problem of living differently,' her teacher replies.

steps.title: Cell theory
steps.body:
- All living organisms are made of cells (Schleiden and Schwann).
- New cells arise only from pre-existing cells (Virchow: *omnis cellula e cellula*).
- The cell is the basic unit of structure and function.

**Prokaryotes** (bacteria): no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles, DNA in a nucleoid, 70S ribosomes, often plasmids. **Eukaryotes** (plants, animals, fungi, protists): true nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm.

steps.title: The organelles and their jobs
steps.body:
- **Plasma membrane**: fluid mosaic model—a lipid bilayer with proteins; selectively permeable.
- **Nucleus**: DNA in chromatin; nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA.
- **Ribosomes**: protein synthesis.
- **Endoplasmic reticulum**: rough ER (with ribosomes) makes proteins for export; smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies.
- **Golgi apparatus**: modifies, packages and dispatches proteins; forms lysosomes.
- **Lysosomes**: digestive enzymes ('suicide bags').
- **Mitochondria**: aerobic respiration, ATP ('powerhouse'); have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes.
- **Chloroplasts** (plants): photosynthesis; also have their own DNA.
- **Vacuole**: large central vacuole in plant cells keeps them turgid.
- **Cell wall** (plants: cellulose; fungi: chitin).

steps.title: Plant vs animal cells
steps.body:
Anaya's onion cells: cell wall ✔, large central vacuole ✔, plastids (chloroplasts in green tissue; onion bulb cells lack them) and a regular shape.

Her cheek cells: no cell wall, small vacuoles if any, centrioles present, irregular shape.

Both have a nucleus, membrane, mitochondria, ER, Golgi and ribosomes.

steps.title: Why mitochondria have their own DNA
steps.body: The **endosymbiotic theory** proposes that mitochondria and chloroplasts descended from free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral cell. Evidence: double membranes, their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and division by fission. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited mainly from the mother.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying prokaryotes have no ribosomes (they have 70S ribosomes).
- Saying all plant cells contain chloroplasts (root and onion-bulb cells don't).
- Mixing up 'cell membrane' and 'cell wall'—every cell has a membrane; only some have a wall.

Answer: rough ER (to make the protein) and the Golgi apparatus (to package and secrete it).

scenes.text: Kabir scrapes his knee playing football in Jalandhar. Within a week, new skin has covered the wound.
At dinner he looks at his two sisters: same parents, yet they look so different from each other.
Two kinds of cell division explain both: mitosis repairs and grows; meiosis makes unique gametes.

steps.title: The cell cycle
steps.body:
Interphase (most of the time): **G₁** (growth), **S** (DNA replication), **G₂** (preparation). Then the **M phase** (mitosis + cytokinesis). Some cells leave the cycle and rest in **G₀** (e.g., many nerve cells).

Checks at each stage stop damaged cells from dividing; failure of these controls can contribute to cancer.

steps.title: Mitosis (equational division)
steps.body:
- **Prophase**: chromatin condenses into chromosomes (two sister chromatids each); nuclear envelope breaks down; spindle forms.
- **Metaphase**: chromosomes line up on the equatorial (metaphase) plate—best stage to count chromosomes.
- **Anaphase**: centromeres split; sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
- **Telophase**: nuclear envelopes re-form; chromosomes decondense.
- **Cytokinesis**: animal cells by a cleavage furrow; plant cells by a cell plate.

Result: 2 genetically identical diploid cells (2n → 2n). Used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.

steps.title: Meiosis (reductional division)
steps.body:
One DNA replication, two divisions, four haploid cells (2n → n).
- **Prophase I**: homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis); **crossing over** at pachytene exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids; chiasmata are visible at diplotene.
- **Metaphase I/Anaphase I**: homologous pairs separate (independent assortment of each pair).
- **Meiosis II**: like mitosis—sister chromatids separate.

Variation comes from crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation. Humans: 2n = 46, gametes n = 23.

steps.title: Counting variation
steps.body: With 23 chromosome pairs, independent assortment alone can produce 2²³ ≈ 8.4 million different chromosome combinations in a person's gametes—before crossing over adds even more. That is why Kabir's sisters differ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking DNA replicates in prophase (it replicates in the S phase).
- Confusing sister chromatids (identical copies) with homologous chromosomes (one from each parent).
- Saying meiosis II halves the chromosome number—meiosis I does that.

Answer: (a) 16; (b) 8.

lessons.title: Mendel and the rules of inheritance

scenes.text: Rohan, 17, in Indore, fails a colour-vision test for a pilot's medical. He is red–green colour blind. His parents both see colours normally.
His grandmother remembers that her own father was colour blind. 'But nobody else in between!' she says.
Rohan's biology teacher, Mr Saxena, draws a pedigree—and Mendel's rules plus X-linkage explain everything.

steps.title: Mendel's laws
steps.body:
Mendel worked on garden peas with clear contrasting traits.
- **Law of dominance**: in a heterozygote (Tt) one allele (T) masks the other (t).
- **Law of segregation**: the two alleles separate during gamete formation; each gamete gets one.
- **Law of independent assortment**: alleles of different genes (on different chromosomes) assort independently.

Monohybrid cross Tt × Tt: genotypes 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt; phenotypes 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
Dihybrid cross RrYy × RrYy: phenotypes 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Test cross (with the recessive homozygote) reveals an unknown genotype: Tt × tt → 1 : 1.

steps.title: Beyond simple dominance
steps.body:
- **Incomplete dominance**: snapdragon red × white → pink F₁; F₂ 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
- **Codominance**: ABO blood groups. Alleles Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant, i is recessive. 6 genotypes, 4 phenotypes (A, B, AB, O).
- **Multiple alleles**: more than two alleles in the population (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i).
- **Polygenic traits**: skin colour, height—many genes, continuous variation.
- **Linkage**: genes close together on one chromosome tend to be inherited together; crossing over separates them.

steps.title: Sex determination and sex-linked traits
steps.body:
Humans: females XX, males XY; the father's sperm (X or Y) determines the child's sex.

**X-linked recessive** traits (red–green colour blindness, haemophilia) appear far more often in males, who have only one X. A carrier mother (XᶜX) passes the allele to half her sons (affected) and half her daughters (carriers).

steps.title: Rohan's pedigree solved
steps.body:
Great-grandfather XᶜY → his daughter (Rohan's grandmother) must be a carrier XᶜX → Rohan's mother received Xᶜ from her: carrier XᶜX, with normal vision → Rohan (son) received Xᶜ from his mother and Y from his father ⇒ XᶜY, colour blind.

For his parents' future children: sons 50% affected, daughters 0% affected but 50% carriers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that a son's X always comes from his mother.
- Writing 3:1 for a test cross (it is 1:1).
- Treating blood group O as dominant.
- Ratios are probabilities for each child, not guarantees for a family of four.

story.title: The DNA that solved a mystery

scenes.text: Forensic scientist Dr Priya Nair in Hyderabad receives a tiny blood spot from a crime scene—far too little DNA to analyse directly.
Her lab copies the DNA millions of times, then compares repeating patterns between samples.
To understand how, intern Arjun must first understand how DNA stores, copies and reads information.

steps.title: DNA structure
steps.body:
- Double helix (Watson and Crick, 1953, using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins).
- Two antiparallel strands (5'→3' and 3'→5') of nucleotides: sugar (deoxyribose), phosphate, base.
- Base pairing: **A=T (2 hydrogen bonds), G≡C (3 hydrogen bonds)** ⇒ Chargaff's rule A = T, G = C.
- Purines A, G; pyrimidines C, T (U in RNA).
- Human genome: about 3 billion base pairs, roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes.

steps.title: Replication
steps.body:
**Semi-conservative** (proven by Meselson and Stahl using ¹⁵N): each new DNA has one old and one new strand.
- Helicase unwinds; DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the **5'→3'** direction.
- **Leading strand**: continuous; **lagging strand**: discontinuous Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase.
- Primers (RNA) start each new strand.

steps.title: Central dogma: transcription and translation
steps.body:
DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein.
- **Transcription**: RNA polymerase reads the template strand; in eukaryotes the primary transcript is processed (introns removed by splicing, 5' cap, poly-A tail).
- **Genetic code**: triplet codons; 64 codons = 61 for amino acids + 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA). **AUG** = start (methionine). The code is nearly universal, degenerate (several codons per amino acid) and non-overlapping.
- **Translation** at ribosomes: tRNA anticodons pair with mRNA codons, bringing amino acids that are joined by peptide bonds.

steps.title: Gene regulation: the lac operon
steps.body: In E. coli, the lac operon's genes (for using lactose) are switched OFF when a repressor binds the operator. When lactose is present, it (as allolactose) inactivates the repressor ⇒ the genes are transcribed. This is an **inducible** system.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
A DNA molecule has 30% adenine. Find the other bases.
- T = A = 30%
- G + C = 40% ⇒ G = C = 20%.

Template DNA strand 3'-TAC GGA TTC-5' → mRNA 5'-AUG CCU AAG-3' → Met–Pro–Lys.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing T in mRNA (RNA uses U).
- Forgetting strands are antiparallel when writing complementary sequences.
- Thinking every codon codes for an amino acid (3 are stop codons).

story.title: The journey of a masala dosa

scenes.text: At a Chennai café, Siddharth bites into a masala dosa: rice-and-lentil batter, potato filling, a little ghee.
Over the next hours, that meal is broken into glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol—small enough to enter his blood.
Let's follow it from mouth to colon.

steps.title: Mouth and stomach
steps.body:
- **Mouth**: chewing; **salivary amylase** begins digesting starch to maltose (about 30% of starch is digested here).
- **Oesophagus**: peristalsis moves food down.
- **Stomach**: HCl (acidic pH, kills microbes, activates pepsinogen to **pepsin**), which breaks proteins into peptides. Mucus protects the stomach lining.

steps.title: Small intestine: the main event
steps.body:
- **Bile** (from the liver, stored in the gall bladder) emulsifies fats—it contains no digestive enzymes.
- **Pancreatic juice**: trypsin (proteins), pancreatic amylase (starch), lipase (fats), nucleases.
- **Intestinal juice** (succus entericus): maltase, lactase, sucrase, dipeptidases complete digestion.
- **Absorption**: villi and microvilli give a huge surface area. Glucose and amino acids enter blood capillaries; fatty acids and glycerol form micelles, are reassembled into chylomicrons and enter the lacteals (lymph).

steps.title: Large intestine
steps.body:
Absorbs water and salts; gut bacteria make some vitamins (e.g., vitamin K). Undigested matter forms faeces.

The liver also stores glycogen, makes bile and detoxifies substances.

steps.title: Health connections
steps.body:
- Lactose intolerance: low lactase in adulthood—milk sugar is fermented by gut bacteria, causing bloating.
- Jaundice: yellowing from bilirubin build-up, often due to liver problems.
- Dehydration from diarrhoea is dangerous—oral rehydration solution (ORS) saves lives. See a doctor if diarrhoea is severe, bloody, or lasts more than a couple of days, or if there are signs of dehydration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying bile digests fats (it only emulsifies them).
- Saying digestion of proteins starts in the mouth (it starts in the stomach).
- Saying fats are absorbed directly into blood capillaries (they enter lacteals first).

scenes.text: Sunita, 17, runs her first half-marathon in Mumbai. By kilometre 15 her heart is racing and she is breathing hard.
Her watch shows a heart rate of 170 beats per minute; at rest it is about 70.
Her lungs and heart are cooperating to deliver oxygen and remove carbon dioxide—let's see how.

steps.title: Breathing mechanics and gas exchange
steps.body:
- **Inspiration**: diaphragm contracts (flattens), external intercostals lift the ribs ⇒ chest volume ↑, pressure ↓, air flows in.
- **Expiration** at rest is mostly passive.
- Tidal volume ≈ 500 mL; vital capacity ≈ 3.5–4.5 L.
- Gas exchange in the **alveoli** by diffusion: O₂ from alveoli (high pO₂) into blood; CO₂ out.

steps.title: Transport of gases
steps.body:
- About **97% of O₂** is carried by haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin; about 3% dissolved in plasma.
- **CO₂**: about 70% as bicarbonate (via carbonic anhydrase in RBCs), 20–25% as carbaminohaemoglobin, about 7% dissolved.
- The oxygen dissociation curve is sigmoid. High CO₂, high H⁺ (low pH) and high temperature in working muscles shift it right—haemoglobin releases more O₂ exactly where Sunita needs it (the Bohr effect).

steps.title: The heart and circulation
steps.body:
- Four chambers; **double circulation**: pulmonary (right ventricle → lungs → left atrium) and systemic (left ventricle → body → right atrium).
- The **SA node** is the pacemaker; impulses pass to the AV node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres.
- Cardiac cycle at about 72 beats/min lasts about 0.8 s. Heart sounds: 'lub' (AV valves close), 'dub' (semilunar valves close).
- **Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate** ≈ 70 mL × 72 ≈ 5 L/min at rest.
- Normal adult blood pressure is around 120/80 mmHg (systolic/diastolic). Persistently high readings (hypertension) need medical attention.

steps.title: Sunita's numbers
steps.body: Rest: 70 mL × 70 beats/min ≈ 4.9 L/min. During the race, with stroke volume rising to about 110 mL and heart rate 170: 110 × 170 ≈ 18.7 L/min—nearly four times more blood delivered every minute.

steps.title: Common mistakes and health note
steps.body:
- Saying arteries always carry oxygenated blood (the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood).
- Saying most CO₂ travels bound to haemoglobin (most travels as bicarbonate).
- Chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness during exercise is a medical emergency—stop and call 112.

scenes.text: Every Tuesday and Friday, Ayaan accompanies his grandfather in Bhopal to a dialysis centre. A machine cleans his blood for four hours.
'My kidneys used to do this all day without me noticing,' his grandfather says.
Ayaan decides to learn exactly what a healthy kidney does—and why it is so hard to replace.

steps.title: The nephron
steps.body:
Each kidney has about a million **nephrons**.
- **Glomerulus + Bowman's capsule**: ultrafiltration under pressure. Filtrate = plasma minus proteins and cells.
- **Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)**: reabsorbs nearly all glucose and amino acids and most water and salts.
- **Loop of Henle**: creates a concentration gradient in the medulla (countercurrent mechanism).
- **Distal tubule and collecting duct**: fine-tune water and salts under hormonal control.

steps.title: The numbers
steps.body: Glomerular filtration rate ≈ 125 mL/min ≈ 180 L/day. About 99% is reabsorbed, leaving roughly 1.5 L of urine per day. Humans excrete nitrogen mainly as **urea** (ureotelic), made in the liver by the ornithine (urea) cycle.

steps.title: Regulation
steps.body:
- **ADH (vasopressin)** from the posterior pituitary makes the collecting duct more permeable to water ⇒ concentrated urine. Low ADH (e.g., in diabetes insipidus) ⇒ large volumes of dilute urine.
- **Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone**: low blood pressure ⇒ renin ⇒ angiotensin II (vasoconstriction) and aldosterone (Na⁺ and water reabsorption).
- **ANF** from the heart opposes this, lowering blood pressure.

steps.title: When kidneys fail
steps.body: Kidney failure lets urea and other wastes build up. **Haemodialysis** filters blood through a semi-permeable membrane against dialysis fluid. A kidney transplant from a matched donor is the long-term option. Diabetes and uncontrolled high blood pressure are major causes of kidney damage, so regular check-ups matter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying proteins are filtered normally (they aren't; protein in urine can signal kidney damage).
- Thinking ADH increases urine volume (it decreases it).
- Confusing the PCT (bulk reabsorption) with the collecting duct (fine-tuning).

lessons.title: Nerves and hormones: the body's control systems

scenes.text: As the board exam paper lands on her desk in Kolkata, Riya's palms sweat and her heart pounds.
Her nerves fired in milliseconds; adrenaline from her adrenal glands keeps her alert for minutes.
Fast wiring and slow chemical messages—two control systems working together.

steps.title: The nerve impulse
steps.body:
- **Resting potential** ≈ −70 mV (inside negative), maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) and K⁺ leak.
- **Action potential**: a stimulus opens Na⁺ channels ⇒ Na⁺ rushes in ⇒ depolarisation; then K⁺ flows out ⇒ repolarisation.
- Myelinated fibres conduct faster by **saltatory conduction** (jumping node to node).
- **Synapse**: an impulse releases neurotransmitters (e.g., acetylcholine) that bind receptors on the next cell.

steps.title: Brain and reflexes
steps.body:
- **Cerebrum**: thinking, memory, voluntary actions, senses. **Cerebellum**: balance and coordination. **Medulla**: breathing, heart rate, swallowing. **Hypothalamus**: temperature, hunger, thirst; controls the pituitary.
- **Reflex arc**: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (interneuron) → motor neuron → effector. Pulling your hand from a hot pan happens before you feel pain.

steps.title: Major hormones
steps.body:
- **Pituitary**: GH (growth), TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH, prolactin; posterior lobe releases ADH and oxytocin.
- **Thyroid**: thyroxine (metabolic rate; iodine needed—deficiency causes goitre).
- **Pancreas (islets)**: insulin from β-cells lowers blood glucose; glucagon from α-cells raises it.
- **Adrenal**: adrenaline/noradrenaline ('fight or flight'), cortisol (stress), aldosterone (salt balance).
- **Gonads**: testosterone; oestrogen and progesterone.

steps.title: Diabetes mellitus
steps.body:
- **Type 1**: the immune system destroys β-cells; insulin injections are needed.
- **Type 2**: the body resists insulin; strongly linked to lifestyle and genetics; managed with diet, exercise and medicines.
Symptoms like excessive thirst, frequent urination and unexplained weight loss need a doctor's evaluation.

steps.title: Calming the exam-hall surge
steps.body: Slow breathing (for example, in for 4 seconds, out for 6) activates the parasympathetic system and calms the adrenaline response. If exam anxiety feels overwhelming, see the Mann (wellbeing) courses or call Tele-MANAS at 14416.

courses.guardianNote: This course covers the Class 12 biology topics of human reproduction and reproductive health: anatomy using correct terms, the menstrual cycle, nightfall (nocturnal emission), fertilisation and pregnancy, contraception, sexually transmitted infections, consent and India's POCSO law. It follows UNESCO's International Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education (2018) and WHO guidance for this age group. story.title: The biology class that nobody giggled in

scenes.text: In a Class 12 classroom in Pune, Dr Kulkarni begins the reproduction chapter. A few students giggle; one hides behind a book.
'I'm a doctor,' she says calmly. 'These are organs, like the heart or kidneys. Using correct names is how we stay healthy and safe.'
By the end of the period, the giggles have turned into good questions.

steps.title: Male reproductive system
steps.body:
- **Testes** (in the scrotum, kept about 2–2.5 °C below body temperature) make sperm in the **seminiferous tubules**; **Leydig cells** make testosterone; **Sertoli cells** nourish developing sperm.
- Sperm mature and are stored in the **epididymis**, travel through the **vas deferens**, and mix with fluids from the **seminal vesicles**, **prostate** and **bulbourethral glands** to form semen.
- The **urethra** carries urine or semen (never both at once) out through the penis.

steps.title: Female reproductive system
steps.body:
- **Ovaries** contain follicles with oocytes and make oestrogen and progesterone.
- **Fallopian tubes (oviducts)**: the fimbriae catch the released ovum; fertilisation usually happens in the **ampulla**.
- **Uterus**: a muscular organ whose inner lining (**endometrium**) thickens each cycle; a pregnancy develops here.
- **Cervix** connects the uterus to the **vagina** (the birth canal).
- **Mammary glands** produce milk after childbirth.

steps.title: Gametogenesis
steps.body:
- **Spermatogenesis** (from puberty, continuous): spermatogonium (2n) → primary spermatocyte → meiosis I → 2 secondary spermatocytes (n) → meiosis II → 4 spermatids → spermiogenesis → 4 sperm.
- **Oogenesis** begins before birth: primary oocytes are arrested in prophase I until puberty. Each cycle, usually one completes meiosis I, producing a secondary oocyte and a small polar body. Meiosis II completes only if a sperm enters. One ovum per oogonium (plus polar bodies).
- Hormones: GnRH (hypothalamus) → FSH and LH (pituitary) → gonads.

steps.title: Variation is normal
steps.body: Bodies differ in size, shape and timing of puberty. Puberty usually begins between about 8 and 13 in girls and 9 and 14 in boys. Comparing yourself with friends or with online images is not a good guide—a doctor is.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying fertilisation happens in the uterus (it usually happens in the ampulla of the fallopian tube).
- Thinking sperm are made in the epididymis (they mature there; they are made in the seminiferous tubules).
- Saying one oogonium gives four ova (it gives one ovum and polar bodies).
